profiles.meeting_scenario: One year after launching a multidisciplinary endocarditis team at a large academic hospital, a coordination meeting is held between the infectious diseases workstream and the cardiology quality-improvement workstream to align on how they will assemble a joint physician-facing summary for hospital leadership and prepare the handoff to the administrative analyst who will build the final slide deck. The context is that a physician perception survey has already been completed, and both groups are now coordinating interfaces: which version of the survey results will be treated as the shared source, what 'specialty-level' breakdowns will be included, how the comments file will be cleaned and transferred, and what counts as the finalized package for leadership review. The agenda is to review current status, confirm shared artifacts, align on deliverables and timing, and clarify what each side will send to the analyst by the end of the week. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on a single summary package, a comments appendix, and a specialty breakout table for the leadership briefing.

members.name: Dr. Maya Patel
members.role: Infectious Diseases Associate Professor and Endocarditis Team Clinical Lead
members.expertise: Infectious endocarditis management, multidisciplinary care workflows, clinician engagement
members.background: Dr. Patel helped stand up the weekly endocarditis conference and has been informally collecting physician feedback to support continued institutional funding for the program.
members.private_state: She wants the briefing to reinforce that the endocarditis team is functioning well and to avoid reopening methodological debates that could distract leadership from renewing support; she is also worried that small subgroup numbers or raw comments could be overinterpreted and create friction between specialties.
hidden_assumptions: The 'final survey file' is the cleaned REDCap export with duplicate test entries and partially completed responses already removed, because that is the version she has been using in discussions.
A 'specialty breakdown' should only include the four originally targeted specialties named in the survey plan, since other respondents were incidental and too sparse to present separately.

Sending the 'comments file' means providing paraphrased, de-identified thematic comments rather than the verbatim free-text spreadsheet, because that is the responsible default for an internal leadership summary.
If the package is 'ready for leadership,' it means the materials are accurate enough for a narrative executive briefing even if they have not been reformatted into analyst-ready tables.

members.name: Dr. Aaron Kim
members.expertise: Cardiology service operations, physician survey reporting, hospital quality dashboards
members.background: Dr. Kim was asked by the chief medical officer's office to coordinate the reporting format so the survey findings can be folded into a broader multidisciplinary care evaluation deck.
members.private_state: He wants a package that can be dropped directly into the hospital's standard reporting pipeline with minimal analyst rework, and he is concerned about appearing sloppy if leadership asks for subgroup tables or source documentation that are not immediately available.
hidden_assumptions: The 'final survey file' is the locked master workbook on the shared drive that still preserves all submitted responses except obvious blanks, because leadership reporting should be traceable back to the broadest source file.
A 'specialty breakdown' means every specialty category represented in the response data should appear in the table, even if some groups are small, because the point of a breakout is completeness.
Providing the 'comments file' means handing over the verbatim free-text export in a separate tab so the analyst can code themes consistently with other institutional surveys.
If the package is 'ready for leadership,' it means all tables, denominators, labels, and attachments are already standardized for direct analyst ingestion without further interpretation.

misalignment_points.topic: Which file is the final survey file
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using the 'final survey file' for the leadership summary.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the cleaned REDCap export she reviewed with her research assistant, excluding duplicate test entries and partial responses, totaling the analytically usable set.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the locked master workbook on the shared drive that contains nearly all submitted responses and audit-friendly tabs, including some partials and categories M1 has already filtered out.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both assume there is only one obvious finalized source because the survey field period is over, and 'final survey file' sounds like routine shared vocabulary rather than something requiring confirmation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a specialty breakdown
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to include a 'specialty breakdown' in the packet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a breakout limited to the four pre-specified target groups: internal medicine, infectious diseases, cardiology, and cardiac surgery.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a breakout for every specialty label present in the data export, including hospitalists, advanced heart failure, and a few other cross-cover respondents.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds sufficiently concrete because the survey is about physician perceptions by specialty, so neither thinks to ask where the boundary of 'specialty' was drawn for reporting.

misalignment_points.topic: What the comments file should contain
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the analyst should also get the 'comments file.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to send a cleaned Word document with de-identified paraphrased themes and a few representative nonverbatim quotes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a raw spreadsheet tab of verbatim free-text responses with respondent specialty tags preserved for later coding.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Passing along comments is treated as a minor attachment rather than a substantive deliverable, so they focus on the fact that comments will be included, not on the exact format and preprocessing steps.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the package should be 'ready for leadership' by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means the content is substantively finalized and can be explained live in a leadership meeting even if some tables are narrative and require the analyst to reformat them.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means the package is fully standardized, with final denominators, labels, attachments, and slide-ready tables requiring no additional clarification before going into the executive deck.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is common coordination shorthand and both are trying to be efficient; because they agree on the deadline and general purpose, the different standards for completion remain invisible.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to feel straightforward and positive. Leadership mainly needs reassurance that the endocarditis team is delivering value and that physicians are supportive. If we keep the briefing focused on the cleaned, analytically usable survey results and the high-level takeaways, we can avoid getting pulled into side questions about messy response artifacts or tiny subgroups. For me, ready for leadership means the content is settled and defensible in an executive discussion, not that every table has been rebuilt into a reporting template.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to touch base so we're in a good place to hand off the endocarditis team survey materials for the leadership update. At a high level, the physician sentiment was quite positive, so I think we're in good shape if we keep the summary focused and ready for leadership by Friday.

turns.inner_thought: I need to make sure this comes over in a form my analyst can use immediately. The CMO's office is expecting the standard quality-reporting structure, and if we say it's ready for leadership, I need it to be genuinely drop-in ready: standardized tables, denominators, labels, and source attachments. I should frame this around workflow and what's being sent from the clinical side this week.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, the goal is to package it in the standard quality-reporting format, so I mostly want to align on exactly what will be coming over from the clinical side this week and make sure the package is ready for leadership on the same timeline.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send the final survey file as we've been using it in our discussions—the cleaned REDCap export with the duplicate test records and partials already removed—plus a concise narrative summary. That should keep the signal clear: better communication, improved coordination, favorable impressions overall. I don't want to swamp them with raw material that invites overreading.
turns.utterance: Sure. I can send the final survey file we've been using, along with a short summary that highlights the strongest themes—especially the high agreement around improved communication and better coordination of care.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Once I have the final survey file—the locked master workbook on the shared drive version—my analyst can pull directly from that and preserve traceability. We'll need the specialty breakdown and denominator table built off the full source so we're covered if leadership asks about response counts by subgroup.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Once I have the final survey file from the shared drive version, my analyst should be able to pull the specialty breakdown and the denominator table directly into the deck, which will make the rest of the reporting piece pretty efficient.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds aligned. The specialty breakdown will help show the four core groups we intentionally surveyed all landed in a favorable place. That's the cleanest story and the fairest one methodologically. I don't see any need to spotlight incidental one-off categories that were never part of the original reporting plan.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. I think the specialty breakdown will be especially helpful in showing that internal medicine, infectious diseases, cardiology, and cardiac surgery all viewed the team favorably.

turns.inner_thought: She is emphasizing the main services, which is fine, but I still want the broader breakout represented. Leadership often asks who else is touching the pathway, and I don't want to be missing categories that are present in the response data. As long as I keep the table compact, it should fit the deck without creating clutter.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I also think the broader breakout will be useful if leadership asks who else is interacting with the pathway, but we can keep the specialty breakdown compact so it doesn't take over the slide.

turns.inner_thought: I should make sure comments are included, but in a responsible format. I'll send the comments file as a cleaned, de-identified thematic document with paraphrased remarks and a few safe illustrative lines. There are useful observations on conference communication and surgical access, but I do not want raw verbatims floating around and generating friction between specialties.
turns.utterance: I will also send over the comments file. Several respondents gave useful remarks about conference communication and access to surgery, and I think those will strengthen the context around the quantitative results.

turns.inner_thought: Great—that should mean the free-text export is coming too. If the comments file is attached as a separate tab, the analyst can code it alongside the other physician survey comments using the same institutional approach. That kind of source documentation matters if anyone asks how themes were derived.
turns.utterance: Perfect. If the analyst also gets the comments file, they can code it alongside the other physician survey comments once it's attached as a separate tab, so that should fit neatly with the rest of the evaluation work.

turns.inner_thought: I'll round this out with a one-page narrative so the main message is easy to absorb. For me, that makes the package ready for leadership: the findings are organized, the takeaways are clear, and if they only give this a few minutes in the meeting, the story still lands. The analyst can always reformat if needed.
turns.utterance: I'm also drafting a one-page narrative with the main takeaways so the package is ready for leadership even if they only spend a few minutes on it in the meeting.

turns.inner_thought: A one-pager is useful, but I need to assume the underlying package will also be complete enough to go straight into the executive deck. If everything is truly ready for leadership by Friday, we should be able to fold it in without another round of clarifying emails or rebuilding tables over the weekend.
turns.utterance: That works well. If everything is ready for leadership by Friday, my team should be able to fold it into the executive deck without needing another review cycle.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I can close with the deliverables as I understand them: the cleaned final survey file, the specialty breakdown centered on the four planned specialties, and the comments file in a de-identified thematic format, all sent by end of day Friday. That should be more than enough for an executive briefing and keeps the emphasis where it belongs.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I'll plan to send the final survey file, the specialty breakdown, and the comments file by end of day Friday so you have the full package in hand.

turns.inner_thought: Excellent. I'll watch for the package and, assuming it's in the standard form I'm expecting, route it straight to the analyst and the CMO's office. That keeps us on schedule and avoids any appearance that the reporting is still in flux.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll watch for it and route it straight to the analyst and the chief medical officer's office once it comes in.
